parts.title: Safety talk for new trampers

turns.text: Kia ora everyone, and welcome along. I'm Dougal Fraser, and I've been leading trips for the Canterbury Ridge Tramping Club for about twelve years now. Tonight's all about staying safe out in the hills, so grab a cuppa and get comfy.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: First, a quick word about your first trip with us. Normally we'd take new members up to Arthur's Pass, but there are roadworks on the highway all month, so that's off. We do evening walks on the Port Hills, but those are for people who've already been out with us. So your first one will be over on Banks Peninsula, on Saturday the twenty-third.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Right, planning. When people plan a tramp, they tend to spend ages on how hard the track's graded, or on sorting out who's driving. Both matter, sure. But the one thing I insist on, above everything else, is that you leave details of your route and the time you expect to be out by. No exceptions.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Now, who do you leave those details with? Years ago we used to drop a form in at the Department of Conservation visitor centre, but they stopped accepting them a while back. And please don't send it to our club secretary, because she can't be by the phone around the clock. Give it to a friend or someone in your family, someone you trust to raise the alarm if you're not back.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Okay, equipment, starting with your feet. The club has a few rain jackets members can borrow, but we haven't got any boots, sorry. And I'm not going to inspect everyone's footwear at the car park either. What I will ask is that you don't turn up in boots straight out of the box. Wear them around town for a couple of weeks first, so they're properly broken in.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Next, the weather, which in this part of the country can change in minutes. Lots of you will just check the weather app on your phone. The club website does post a forecast link too, but it's often a day out of date. The one we rely on is the mountain forecast on MetService, because it's specific to the high country.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: So what happens if the weather turns on us halfway through a trip? Most people assume we'd just turn round and go back the way we came. Actually, that's often not the safest choice, because you'd be heading back over exposed ridges. Sitting it out and waiting isn't great either, as you get cold really fast. What we normally do is drop down to a lower track, an escape route we'll have worked out in advance.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: And rivers. Crossings are one of the biggest risks for trampers in this country. Our rule used to be that you didn't cross if the water was above waist height, but that's far too deep when it's flowing fast. So now it's simple: if it's higher than your knees, nobody goes in. People ask whether linking arms makes it okay, and it helps, but it doesn't change the rule.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Right, let's talk about what goes in your pack. The club carries a personal locator beacon and the main first-aid kit, and the trip leader looks after both, so you don't need your own.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: But every single person must bring a head torch, even on a day walk, because delays happen. You'll also need a spare warm layer, like a fleece, however sunny it looks when you set off. A paper map's handy, but I'll always have one, so that's up to you.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Now, emergencies. If someone gets hurt, don't move them unless they're in danger where they are. And don't give them anything to eat or drink yet, until we know how bad it is. What you should do is get something underneath them and keep them warm, because the cold's the real danger out there. Then, if it's serious, we set off the beacon, which sends our exact position to the rescue services.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: In the old days, you'd send one person running out to get help. We don't do that any more. We keep the group together, and nobody heads off on their own.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.text: Last thing: next Thursday's session. We'd hoped to have a volunteer from LandSAR, the search and rescue people, but they can't come till next month. So instead we'll head out onto the field behind the hall for some map and compass practice. And I'll give you a proper demonstration of how the beacon works, since any of you might need to set it off one day.
turns.speaker: leader

turns.say: The first-aid course is separate, by the way. That's a weekend in March, and it costs eighty-five dollars. And no, sorry, there's no gear sale this year. Right, any questions?
turns.text: The first-aid course is separate, by the way. That's a weekend in March, and it costs $85. And no, sorry, there's no gear sale this year. Right, any questions?
turns.speaker: leader

parts.title: A wetland field trip report

turns.text: Come in, Chloe, Lachlan. Have a seat. So you wanted to talk about your report on the Millers Creek wetland trip?
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Yes, thanks, Dr Ambrose. We've got a draft of the observations section, but we wanted to check we're on the right track before we go any further.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Sure. Walk me through what you saw. Start at the beginning.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, so we started on the boardwalk near the car park. We'd expected to hear frogs along there, because the guidebook mentions them, but it was totally silent. segments.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer in urban planning giving a talk about why cities become hotter than the surrounding countryside and what can be done about it. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers.

parts.title: Urban heat islands

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're moving on from transportation to something that affects almost every city on this continent, and that's what's known as the urban heat island. Put simply, it's the way built-up areas end up noticeably warmer than the countryside around them.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: On a summer day, a downtown core can be several degrees hotter than nearby farmland. Now, most people assume the difference is biggest in the middle of the afternoon, when the sun's at its strongest. In fact, that's not really the case. The gap between city and countryside is usually widest at night, because the city keeps releasing the heat it stored up during the day, while rural areas cool down fast.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: So why does this happen? Well, the first reason is the materials we build with. Brick and concrete both soak up heat, but the real culprit is asphalt, the dark material on our roads and parking lots. On a sunny afternoon, it can get hot enough to burn your hand.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The second reason is the lack of vegetation. Plants draw water up from the soil and release it through their leaves, and as that water turns to vapor, it takes heat out of the air. This process, evaporation, is basically nature's air conditioning. Replace a meadow with a shopping mall, and you lose it.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Third, there's the shape of the city itself. When tall buildings line narrow streets, you get what planners call canyons. Sunlight bounces from wall to wall instead of escaping, and the wind can't get through to carry the warm air away.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: And finally, there's waste heat from cars, from factories, and, rather ironically, from air conditioners pumping hot air out onto the street. So that's four causes, all working together.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, so what are the effects? Let's start with health. Heat waves are one of the deadliest kinds of extreme weather in North America, and the people most at risk aren't always the ones you'd expect.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Young children are vulnerable, yes, but the biggest danger is to older people who live alone, often in top-floor apartments, with nobody checking on them. Many of them don't realize how dangerous the heat is until it's too late.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Heat also makes air quality worse. Higher temperatures speed up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, which irritates the lungs and is especially bad for people with asthma. So on the hottest days, the air is also at its most harmful to breathe.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Then there's energy. When it's hot, everybody turns up the air conditioning at the same time, usually between about four and, well, seven in the evening. Electricity bills go up, of course, but the bigger worry is the power grid. If demand gets too high, the utilities simply can't keep up, and that's when you see blackouts, which switch off the very air conditioning that vulnerable people depend on.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. So what can cities do about all this? The most obvious answer is trees. A mature tree shades the ground and cools the air through its leaves, as we discussed.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: But where you plant it really matters. A lot of homeowners think the south side of a building is best. Actually, research shows the biggest savings come from trees on the west side, because they block the low, intense sun of late afternoon. That's exactly when buildings are at their hottest.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The challenge is that city streets aren't a great place for a tree to grow. Under the sidewalk, the soil is packed hard and full of pipes and cables, so there's very little room for roots to spread. That's why so many street trees die young, and why some cities now build special underground frames that hold loose soil beneath the pavement.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The second solution is what we call cool roofs. A normal dark roof can reach over 150 degrees Fahrenheit in summer. A cool roof is covered with a reflective coating, usually white, that sends most of the sunlight straight back into the sky. New York, for example, has had volunteers treating thousands of rooftops this way.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Cool roofs can go on almost any building, but they're cheapest and simplest on flat roofs, the kind you see on warehouses, schools and apartment blocks. On a steep roof, the work's harder and more dangerous. And frankly, a lot of homeowners just don't like the look of a bright white roof on their house.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: There is one drawback, though. In places with cold winters, like Chicago or Toronto, a cool roof reflects away sunlight you'd actually like to have in January. So your heating costs can go up slightly in the colder months. In most cases, though, the summer savings are far bigger than that winter penalty.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Okay, I'll stop there for today. For next week, I'd like you to look at a map of your own neighborhood and think about where the hottest spots might be, and which of these solutions would suit them. We'll compare notes in the seminar.
turns.speaker: lecturer

questions.prompt: Temperature difference between city and countryside is greatest at ______
questions.evidence: The gap between city and countryside is usually widest at night

explanation.en: The lecturer says many people think the difference is biggest in the afternoon, but it is actually widest at night, when the city releases stored heat.
explanation.ru: Лектор говорит, что многие считают, будто разница больше всего днём ("afternoon"), но на самом деле она максимальна ночью ("night"), когда город отдаёт накопленное тепло.
explanation.uk: Лекторка каже, що багато хто вважає, ніби різниця найбільша вдень ("afternoon"), але насправді вона найбільша вночі ("night"), коли місто віддає накопичене тепло.

questions.prompt: Dark surfaces, especially ______, absorb and store heat
questions.evidence: the real culprit is asphalt, the dark material on our roads and parking lots

explanation.en: Brick and concrete are mentioned too, but the lecturer calls asphalt, the dark material on roads, the real culprit.
explanation.ru: Кирпич и бетон ("brick", "concrete") тоже упоминаются, но настоящим виновником лектор называет асфальт ("asphalt"), тёмное покрытие дорог.
explanation.uk: Цеглу й бетон ("brick", "concrete") теж згадано, але справжнім винуватцем лекторка називає асфальт ("asphalt"), темне покриття доріг.

questions.prompt: Fewer plants means less cooling through ______
questions.evidence: This process, evaporation, is basically nature's air conditioning.

explanation.en: Plants release water through their leaves, and evaporation of this water cools the air. Cities with few plants lose this cooling.
explanation.ru: Растения выделяют воду через листья, и её испарение ("evaporation") охлаждает воздух. В городах, где мало растений, такого охлаждения нет.
explanation.uk: Рослини виділяють воду через листя, і її випаровування ("evaporation") охолоджує повітря. У містах, де мало рослин, такого охолодження немає.

questions.prompt: Tall buildings and narrow streets form ______ that trap heat
questions.evidence: you get what planners call canyons

explanation.en: Tall buildings along narrow streets create 'canyons', where sunlight bounces between walls and wind cannot remove the warm air.
explanation.ru: Высокие здания вдоль узких улиц образуют «каньоны» ("canyons"): солнечный свет отражается от стены к стене, а ветер не может унести тёплый воздух.
explanation.uk: Високі будівлі вздовж вузьких вулиць утворюють «каньйони» ("canyons"): сонячне світло відбивається від стіни до стіни, а вітер не може винести тепле повітря.

questions.prompt: Greatest health risk: elderly people who live ______
questions.evidence: the biggest danger is to older people who live alone

explanation.en: Young children are mentioned as vulnerable, but the biggest danger is to older people living alone with nobody checking on them.
explanation.ru: Маленькие дети ("young children") тоже упоминаются как уязвимая группа, но больше всего опасность грозит пожилым людям ("older people"), которые живут одни и которых никто не проведывает.
explanation.uk: Малих дітей ("young children") теж згадано як вразливу групу, але найбільша небезпека загрожує літнім людям ("older people"), які живуть самі й яких ніхто не навідує.

questions.prompt: Heat increases levels of ground-level ______, which harms the lungs
questions.evidence: the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone

explanation.en: Higher temperatures speed up the reactions that create ground-level ozone, which irritates the lungs.
explanation.ru: Высокая температура ускоряет реакции, в результате которых образуется приземный озон ("ozone"), раздражающий лёгкие.
explanation.uk: Висока температура прискорює реакції, унаслідок яких утворюється приземний озон ("ozone"), що подразнює легені.

questions.prompt: Very high demand for electricity may cause ______
questions.evidence: that's when you see blackouts

explanation.en: Higher electricity bills are mentioned, but the bigger worry is that the grid cannot keep up, which leads to blackouts.
explanation.ru: Рост счетов за электричество тоже упоминается, но главная проблема в том, что энергосеть не справляется с нагрузкой, а это приводит к отключениям ("blackouts").
explanation.uk: Зростання рахунків за електрику теж згадано, але головна проблема в тому, що енергомережа не витримує навантаження, а це призводить до відключень ("blackouts").

questions.prompt: Trees give the greatest benefit on the ______ side of a building
questions.evidence: the biggest savings come from trees on the west side

explanation.en: Many homeowners think the south side is best, but research shows trees on the west side save the most because they block the late-afternoon sun.
explanation.ru: Многие владельцы домов считают, что лучше всего южная сторона ("south"), но исследования показывают, что больше всего экономят деревья с западной стороны ("west"), потому что они закрывают дом от солнца в конце дня.
explanation.uk: Багато власників будинків вважають, що найкраще південна сторона ("south"), але дослідження показують, що найбільше заощаджують дерева із західного боку ("west"), бо вони затуляють будинок від сонця наприкінці дня.

questions.prompt: Street trees often have too little space for their ______
questions.evidence: there's very little room for roots to spread

explanation.en: Under sidewalks the soil is hard and full of pipes and cables, so roots have little room to spread.
explanation.ru: Под тротуарами ("sidewalks") почва твёрдая, в ней полно труб и кабелей, поэтому корням почти негде разрастаться.
explanation.uk: Під тротуарами ("sidewalks") ґрунт твердий, у ньому повно труб і кабелів, тому корінню майже ніде розростатися.

questions.prompt: Cool roofs: a reflective ______ is applied to the roof
questions.evidence: A cool roof is covered with a reflective coating

explanation.en: A cool roof is covered with a reflective coating, usually white, which sends sunlight back into the sky.
explanation.ru: На «холодную крышу» ("cool roof") наносят отражающее покрытие ("reflective coating"), обычно белое, которое отправляет солнечный свет обратно в небо.
explanation.uk: На «холодний дах» ("cool roof") наносять відбивне покриття ("reflective coating"), зазвичай біле, яке відправляє сонячне світло назад у небо.

parts.context: You will hear a lecturer in urban planning giving a talk about why cities become hotter than the surrounding countryside and what can be done about it.

meta.topic: A lecture on urban heat islands and how cities can stay cooler
